articles.title: Ready to move out?

body.support:
Moving out takes lots of reading.

**1. Budget first.** Add up your money. Take away **rent**, **bills**, food and transport. Is anything left?

**2. Read the ad.**

- Rent per week, or per month?
- How much is the **bond**?
- Are bills included?
- How long is the **lease**?

**3. Compare the total.** Cheaper rent isn't always cheaper. Add bills and transport.

**4. Go to the inspection.** Check the heating, hot water and locks.

**5. Know the rules.** In Victoria, from **2026**, everyone uses the **same application form**. Agents can't charge a fee to apply. They can't ask you to pay more rent than the ad says.

**6. Read the lease.** Your bond goes to the **RTBA**, not the landlord. Take photos when you move in.

Need help? Ask **Tenants Victoria**.
body.core:
Moving out, whether it's next year or in five, takes more reading than most people expect.

**1. Budget first.** Before you look at a single ad, work out what you can afford. Add up your income, then take away **rent**, **bills** (power, gas, water, internet), food, transport and phone. Something should be left for savings and surprises. If it isn't, the place is too expensive, however nice it looks.

**2. Read the ad closely.**

- Is the rent **per week** or per month?
- How much is the **bond**?
- Are **bills** included, or extra?
- Is it furnished?
- How long is the lease? A **fixed term** (like 12 months) locks you in.

**3. Compare the total.** A room with cheaper rent can cost more once you add bills and transport. Always compare the **total weekly cost**.

**4. Inspect it.** Go to the **inspection**. Check the things that matter: heating, hot water, locks, mould, and whether you could get to school, TAFE or work.

**5. Apply, and know the rules.** In Victoria, from **31 March 2026**, every private rental application must use the **standard rental application form** from Consumer Affairs Victoria. Agents can't charge you a fee to apply, can't ask for information that isn't on the form, and can't ask you to offer more than the advertised rent. If you're under 18, you can still sign a lease, and a **rental provider** can't refuse you just because of your age.

**6. Read the lease before you sign.** You must be given a copy. Check how long it's for, the rent and when it's due, and who pays which bills. Your bond must go to the **Residential Tenancies Bond Authority** (RTBA), not the landlord's pocket. When you move in, fill in the **condition report** carefully and take photos. It protects your bond when you move out.

Not sure? **Tenants Victoria** and **Consumer Affairs Victoria** give free advice.
body.extend:
Renting involves a series of important texts: ads, applications, leases and condition reports.

**1. Establish affordability.** Work out your income. Subtract **rent**, **bills** (utilities and internet), food, transport and phone, and leave a buffer. If there's no buffer left, the place is unaffordable, however good it looks.

**2. Read advertisements precisely.** Note the rent period, the **bond**, whether **bills** are included, the furnishing and the lease type. A **fixed term** commits you for its whole length.

**3. Compare total cost.** Bills and transport can cancel out lower rent. Compare the **total weekly cost**, not the headline figure.

**4. Inspect** against priorities: heating, hot water, security, damp and mould, and access to study or work.

**5. Apply within the rules.** From **31 March 2026**, Victorian private rental applications must use Consumer Affairs Victoria's **standard rental application form**. Rental providers and agents can't charge application fees, ask for information beyond the form, or seek offers above the advertised rent. People under 18 can generally sign a lease for somewhere to live. A **rental provider** can't reject an application on age alone.

**6. Read the lease before signing.** You must get a copy. Check the term, the rent and when it's due, and who pays the utilities. The bond must be lodged with the **Residential Tenancies Bond Authority** (RTBA). A detailed **condition report**, with photos, is your evidence when you ask for your bond back.

**Tenants Victoria** and **Consumer Affairs Victoria** provide free guidance.

caseStudies.title: The new rental application rules

body.support:
Applying to rent used to be messy. Every agent used a different form. Some charged fees.

From **31 March 2026**, Victoria has **one form** for everyone.

What it means:

- Agents must use the **same form**.
- They **can't** ask for things that aren't on it.
- No one can charge you to apply.
- Agents can't ask you to pay **more rent** than the ad says.

These rules help first-time renters. But you need to know them.
body.core:
Applying for a rental used to be messy. Every agent had their own form. Some asked for things renters felt were unfair. Some websites charged renters to apply.

Victoria changed the rules. From **31 March 2026**, every application for a private rental in Victoria must use **one standard form**, made by **Consumer Affairs Victoria**.

Here's what that means:

- Rental providers and agents **must** use the standard form. They can't add their own questions, or take any out.
- They **can't** ask you for information that isn't on the form.
- No one can charge you a **fee** to apply. That includes fees for checking your identity or background, and fees from rental websites.
- **Rental bidding** is banned. Places must be advertised at a fixed rent, and agents can't ask you to offer more.

The rules are designed to make applying fairer, especially for people renting for the first time. But rules only help if you know them. If an agent asks for something that's not on the form, or wants a fee, you can say no, and get advice.
body.extend:
Victorian rental applications used to vary a lot. Agents used their own forms. Some asked for information renters thought was too personal. Some websites charged applicants.

From **31 March 2026**, all applications for private rentals must use **Consumer Affairs Victoria's standard rental application form**.

- Rental providers and agents **must** use this form. They can't add or remove questions.
- They **can't** ask for information that isn't on the form.
- No one, including rental websites, can charge **application fees**. That includes fees for identity, background or other checks.
- **Rental bidding** is banned. Properties must be advertised at a fixed rent. Agents can't invite or accept offers above it.

The reforms make an important text the same for everyone. That reduces the advantage of applicants who know how to work an informal system. But a rule only protects people who know about it. That's why reading the rules is part of renting.

**Subject:** Enquiry: 2/14 Station Street, Sebastopol

I work part time and can provide references and payslips.

Thank you for your time.

Yours sincerely,
Kai Wilson

teacher.overview: A Crossroads capstone combining Money Moves and Get Sorted. Students build a move-out budget, read and compare rental ads by total weekly cost, learn Victoria's current application rules (the standard rental application form from 31 March 2026, no application fees, no rental bidding, no refusal on age alone), unpack lease language, and write a formal enquiry to an agent. The case study is Consumer Affairs Victoria's guidance on the new application rules.

Download the Victorian standard lease and rental application form from Consumer Affairs Victoria to show students.
Check the rules haven't changed since this course was written (2026).

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** what you can afford (income minus rent, bills, food, transport, phone, savings). Ad: rent period, bond, bills, furnishing, lease length. Agents can't charge application fees, ask for information not on the standard form, or invite offers above the advertised rent.

**Rental ad:** 1 rent (per week); 2 bond (goes to the RTBA); 3 bills extra (ask how much); 4 unfurnished; 5 fixed term (12 months); 6 inspection; 7 application (standard form, no fees).

**Compare:** Room A $255 a week ($13,260 a year); Room B $270 a week ($14,040 a year). Room A is cheaper overall, and closer.

**Sort:** $40 fee — not allowed; standard form — allowed (required); bidding — not allowed; copy of the lease — allowed (required); refusal for being 17 — not allowed; landlord keeps the bond — not allowed.

**Unpack (samples):** I pay for power, gas, water and internet; the rental provider must lodge my bond with the RTBA; if I damage the place beyond normal wear, money can be taken from my bond; to end the lease, someone must give notice in writing.

realityCheck: **Most students won't move out soon.** Frame it as preparing for the future, and as helping family members who rent.
**Housing can be a sensitive topic.** Some students are in insecure housing or already living away from family. Follow your wellbeing procedures if a student is at risk of homelessness.
**Rules change.** Check Consumer Affairs Victoria before teaching; this course was written in 2026, just after the new application rules began.
**Real costs vary a lot.** Use local listings so the numbers mean something.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It combines budgeting, comparing, rights and formal writing for a decision students will face.
